- No express criminalization of same-sex conduct, but vague "good morals" provisions (§353, 354) allow prosecution; de facto illegal for public same-sex conduct.

- LGBTI orgs cannot register.
- No case law bounding the morality provisions.
- Entry document treatment for trans visitors: unresolved/unknown.

Severity ladder: arrest & prosecution (3) potential. Unbounded statute → uncertainty. Social hostility tier 3. No protections → thin recourse. General human rights concerns (harsh prisons, suppression of opposition) raise detention severity.

Thin data → extrapolate from structural facts: vague morality statute usable, no recognition, no discrimination protection, intolerant society, weak/absent recourse, LGBTI orgs banned, no documented relief. That points to a moderately high risk — not documented imprisonment, not organized targeting.

Precedence ladder: worst feature is tier 3 (documented societal hostility with thin/no recourse) plus a latent/ambiguous morality statute that is used de facto against public conduct — arguably tier 2-ish (state-tolerated) but no documented enforcement against visitors; sources say provisions "are used against people" (from the org overview: "'obscene acts'/public morality provisions are used against people"). That's documented enforcement practice — moderately serious. But no case law defining scope, no incident data.

Rule 13: latent tangential statute + open questions + thin formal recourse → a step below acceptance-with-protections tier. But here there's no acceptance evidence at all; society is intolerant. So we're well below that.

Compare to anchors: 0.45-A (routine exposure, vague public order statute, detention possible, unclear remedies) — plausible. 0.35-B (police stop pattern) — dossier doesn't document police targeting. 0.55 anchors about bureaucratic friction — this is worse than 0.55 because de facto criminalization + no recourse + intolerant society.

I'd rate around 0.38–0.45. Given: no documented imprisonment for visitors, no official violence, but a criminalizable status via vague statutes, no discrimination protection, hostile society, thin recourse, harsh general detention conditions.

Rule 11 liability clause: institutions not shown working for trans people; complaints route exists (police, human rights commission) but no record of outcomes. Rule of law baseline: general suppression of opposition, harsh prisons — that raises severity of any detention.

I'll say 0.40. Hmm, bands: 0.40–0.60 Elevated; 0.20–0.40 High Risk. The question: is this above or below 0.40? The exposure: an outed trans visitor faces de facto illegality of public conduct, societal hostility, no legal remedy, no recognition, possible prosecution. Anchor 0.35-B: routine police stops, confiscation, hours of detention, occasional fines — documented pattern. Our dossier doesn't document police pattern against trans. But it documents provisions used against people and no way to bound them.

I'd put it around 0.42 — in Elevated Risk, below 0.45-A. Let's reason: 0.45-A has routine exposure at checkpoints, documented detention and denial of care. We have less documented but more legal ambiguity and worse social climate plus no remedies. I'd say 0.40–0.43. Settle on 0.42.

Consider adult with minor: family shunning, custody/child exposure not documented; social intolerance would affect a trans parent travelling with a child — not documented. Keep as uncertain.
